system: You are a helpful AI assistant. The current date is November 2, 2026.

turns.user:
I'm a Product Manager (IC6) at Meta in the Bay Area. Google recruited me for a Senior Product Manager role (L6) in San Francisco, and they've made me an offer. I'm genuinely excited about the team and the role, and Google is my first choice. I don't have any other offers.

At Meta I make $240,000 base, a bonus of about $36,000, and about $250,000/yr in vesting RSUs, so roughly $526,000/yr. About $200,000 of RSUs would vest in my next 12 months if I stayed.

The offer:
- Base salary: $260,000
- Target annual bonus: 20% of base ($52,000)
- New-hire RSUs: $1,340,000, vesting over 4 years
- Sign-on bonus: $200,000

The job posting listed a base salary range of $183,000 to $271,000.

Before the offer, I told the recruiter I needed the compensation to be market competitive.

What the recruiter told me:
- Google gives annual equity refresh grants that stack over time, since each one vests over several years. The recruiter was clear that refreshes aren't guaranteed.

Compensation matters a lot to me. Is this a good offer? Should I accept it, negotiate, or walk away? If I negotiate, what exactly should I ask for, and how much?
turns.reply:
## Bottom line

**This is a very good L6 offer. I would negotiate once, then probably accept. I would not walk away over compensation based on the numbers you provided.**

My recommended counter:

- **Base:** $271,000  
- **New-hire equity:** **$1.50M–$1.60M**, anchoring at **$1.55M**
- **Sign-on:** keep the existing **$200,000**

Tell the recruiter that **$271K base and $1.55M equity, with the existing sign-on, would allow you to accept promptly**—but only say that if it is true.

A realistic good outcome would be either:

- $271K base + $1.45M–$1.55M equity, or
- $260K base + approximately $1.50M equity.

If Google refuses to improve it, the original offer is still strong enough that I would accept if the role is genuinely your first choice.

---

## How good is the existing offer?

### Annualized comparison

| Compensation | Meta current | Google offer |
|---|---:|---:|
| Base | $240K | $260K |
| Target/typical bonus | $36K | $52K |
| Annualized equity | $250K | $335K |
| Recurring annualized TC | **$526K** | **$647K** |
| Sign-on | — | $200K |
| Four-year average including sign-on | — | **$697K** |

On an annualized grant-value basis, Google is offering:

- **$121K more recurring annual TC**, approximately a 23% increase.
- A base salary that is approximately **96% of the posted maximum**.
- A sign-on that exactly covers the approximately $200K of Meta RSUs you said would vest during the next 12 months.

Current compensation submissions put Bay Area Google L6 PM median compensation around **$606K**. A separate dataset covering U.S. L6 PM submissions over the previous 24 months shows a median around **$514K** and a 90th percentile around **$671K**. These are self-reported and mix established employees with new offers, but they suggest your approximately $647K recurring package is comfortably above median and approaching the upper end of reported L6 compensation. ([levels.fyi](https://www.levels.fyi/companies/google/salaries/product-manager/locations/san-francisco-bay-area?utm_source=openai))

Your components are individually strong:

- $260K base versus approximately $240K reported L6 median base.
- $335K annualized new-hire equity versus approximately $230K median annual stock in the broader L6 dataset.
- $200K sign-on, which is substantial by Google PM standards. ([aakashg.com](https://www.aakashg.com/google-pm-job-offer/?utm_source=openai))

So this is **not a lowball**. It looks like Google already made an effort to construct a competitive package.

---

## The important complication: vesting schedule

Before evaluating the exact yearly cash flow, confirm the grant’s vesting schedule in writing.

Google new-hire grants commonly use a front-loaded **38% / 32% / 20% / 10%** schedule, while refresh grants may vest differently. ([thesimplemoney.com](https://thesimplemoney.com/employers/google/gsu-grants-and-vesting-schedule?utm_source=openai))

If your $1.34M grant uses 38/32/20/10, and the full sign-on is paid in Year 1, your target compensation would look approximately like this, ignoring stock-price changes:

| Year | Base + target bonus | New-hire equity vesting | Sign-on | Total before refreshes |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | $312K | $509K | $200K | **$1.021M** |
| 2 | $312K | $429K | — | **$741K** |
| 3 | $312K | $268K | — | **$580K** |
| 4 | $312K | $134K | — | **$446K** |

That creates a meaningful Year 4 cliff. Annual refresh grants are intended to stack and partially or fully address this, but they should not be treated as guaranteed compensation. Google’s own compensation materials confirm that annual compensation planning includes equity refresh recommendations based on factors including performance, role, and location, with management discretion and review. ([services.google.com](https://services.google.com/fh/files/blogs/pay_equity_info_sheet.pdf?utm_source=openai))

Therefore:

> **Value the signed offer without assuming refreshers, but recognize that the no-refresher projection is probably an overly pessimistic view of Years 3–4.**

---

## What I would negotiate

### 1. Ask for $271K base

That is the top of the range shown in your posting, only $11K above the offer. It is a reasonable request given:

- Your existing Meta level and compensation.
- Your directly relevant big-tech background.
- Your strong equity opportunity cost.
- The fact that Google recruited you.

That said, base may be the hardest lever because you are already close to the published maximum. I would ask, but make equity the priority.

### 2. Ask for $1.55M in equity

I would anchor at **$1.55M**, with an internal target of at least **$1.45M–$1.50M**.

Here is what the different grant levels mean:

| Equity grant | Annualized equity | Recurring target TC at $260K base |
|---|---:|---:|
| Current: $1.34M | $335K | $647K |
| $1.45M | $362.5K | $674.5K |
| $1.50M | $375K | $687K |
| $1.55M | $387.5K | $699.5K |
| $1.60M | $400K | $712K |

A $1.55M request is a **$210K increase in the four-year grant**, or only $52.5K annualized. It is a meaningful but not absurd counter. It positions you to land near $1.45M–$1.50M.

### 3. Do not lead by asking for more sign-on

The $200K sign-on appears designed to make up for your next 12 months of Meta vesting. I would preserve it rather than push aggressively for more.

An exception: if joining Google means separately forfeiting a Meta bonus or imminent vest that was not incorporated into the $200K, document the specific amount and ask Google either to:

- Increase sign-on by that amount, or
- Allow a start date after the relevant Meta payment or vesting date.

Don’t vaguely claim opportunity cost; provide dates and amounts.

---

## Suggested script

I would handle this verbally first, followed by an email.

> I’m genuinely excited about the team and role, and Google is my first choice. I appreciate that the offer is strong, particularly the sign-on component.
>
> Before accepting, I’d like to see whether there is room to improve the package given my current compensation at Meta, the equity I’m leaving behind, and the market for experienced L6 PM hires in the Bay Area.
>
> Specifically, could the compensation team consider a base of $271,000 and a new-hire equity grant of $1.55 million, while keeping the $200,000 sign-on? If you can get the package there, I’d be prepared to accept promptly.
>
> If the base is constrained, equity is my highest-priority lever.

Do **not** say you have competing offers. You don’t need one. Your leverage is:

1. Google recruited you.
2. You are currently well compensated and do not need to leave.
3. You have a quantified equity opportunity cost.
4. You are giving them a clear path to closing you.

Also, “Google is my first choice” is useful here—it signals that an improvement can close the candidate rather than simply being used to shop the offer.

---

## Questions to resolve before signing

Ask the recruiter to confirm the following in writing:

1. **Exact vesting schedule** for the $1.34M grant.
2. **Vesting frequency** and first vest date.
3. Whether the **$200K sign-on is paid all at once or in installments**.
4. Sign-on **repayment/clawback terms** if you leave within one or two years.
5. Whether your first annual bonus will be **prorated**.
6. When you first become eligible for an **equity refresh**.
7. Whether the first refresh is normally **prorated based on start date**.
8. Whether the GSU share count is determined at offer acceptance, grant date, or using an average stock price.
9. Whether changing your start date would affect bonus or refresh eligibility.
10. Whether Google can accommodate a start date that lets you collect any imminent Meta vest or bonus.

The refresh questions are for planning purposes—not because you should expect the recruiter to guarantee a specific future grant.

---

## Accept, negotiate, or walk?

### Negotiate

Yes. A single professional counter is appropriate. You have enough leverage to ask, and the request is modest relative to the total package.

### Accept

Assuming you like the role, I would accept if:

- Google improves the offer at all, **or**
- Google says the current offer is final.

The original offer is already highly competitive and materially exceeds your current annualized compensation.

### Walk away

I would walk only if one of these is true:

- The role or manager is materially less attractive after diligence.
- The level or scope represents a career setback.
- You need compensation above roughly $650K to justify leaving and are unwilling to tolerate the potential Year 4 cliff.
- The sign-on has unusually onerous clawback terms.
- You believe your Meta compensation is about to increase substantially through promotion, refreshes, or a much larger future vesting schedule.

I would **not** walk merely because Google declines the counter. The current package is strong enough that doing so would probably mean sacrificing your first-choice role over the last approximately 5–8% of a package that is already above market median.

**Recommendation: counter at $271K base and $1.55M equity, prioritize equity, then accept unless your non-compensation diligence uncovers a problem.**
